- **Static sag: 35 mm (1.38 in)** — bike upright, no rider.
- **Rider sag: 105 mm (4.13 in)** — you aboard in full riding gear, feet on the pegs.

Measure both from the rear axle to the same fender mark, subtracting each reading from the measurement with the rear wheel hanging free. Set rider sag first, then check static sag: too little static sag means the shock spring is too soft; too much means it is too stiff.

That combination often means the fork is **too soft and riding deep in its stroke**—backing compression out can make both problems worse.

1. **Fork air:** check it cold with the front wheel off the ground; if below GASGAS’s standard **10.4 bar (151 psi)**, restore that reference before testing. Bleed the outer chambers through the bleeder screws, not the main air valve.
2. **Fork compression:** if pressure is correct, try **2 clicks in from your current position** for more hold-up. The stock reference is **12 clicks out**; if you’re there now, test **10 out**. Leave rebound unchanged.

Use the same chop and a familiar landing. You want less dive and bottoming without sharper hits through the bars; undo the compression change if deflection increases. If support improves but chop stays harsh, check fork alignment and seal drag before chasing more clicks or oil volume.

**What do you weigh in riding gear?** That decides whether the stock air-pressure reference needs moving upward or downward.

**Changes to try, one at a time:**
- **Fork air pressure:** If below the stock reference, restore to 10.4 bar (151 psi), checked cold with the front wheel unloaded.
- **Fork compression:** With air pressure established, turn 2 clicks in from the current setting; from 12 to 10 clicks out if currently stock.
Harsh chop plus bottoming often means the fork is riding too deep, not that it needs softer compression. Check cold air pressure first, then test slightly firmer compression.

Your fork needs more support under braking—check its air spring before adding compression damping.

- **Fork air:** GASGAS’s stock reference is **10.4 bar (151 psi)**. Check it cold with the front wheel off the ground; correct it to that reference if low. Rider weight may call for a different pressure.
- **Fork compression:** try **2 clicks in from your current position**. If it is at the stock 12 clicks out, go **from 12 to 10 clicks out**. Leave rebound unchanged; stock rebound is 12 out. Count from lightly seated, never forced.

Retest the same braking zone for a few controlled laps. You want less dive without the front becoming sharp or losing grip; undo the compression change if that happens. Check rear balance too: stock targets are **105 mm rider sag and 35 mm static sag**—a rear riding too high loads the fork.

For braking, stand and brace with your legs before squeezing the brake, keeping hips back over the pegs and arms loose. Practice five progressive straight-line stops, not harder brake grabs.

**One click at a time** is the best testing step on your 2022 CRF250R—testers consistently find this suspension sensitive to small changes. Two clicks can make a difference easier to feel, but start with one.

- **Clockwise/in:** more damping—firmer compression or slower rebound.
- **Counterclockwise/out:** less damping—softer compression or faster rebound.

Write down your starting position, change one adjuster, then ride the same section for a few laps at a consistent pace. Keep it only if the feel improves; otherwise return to baseline before trying something else.

The shock’s **high-speed compression uses turns, not clicks**; common practice is a small **1/12-turn** test on a sensitive setup like this.
Change one click at a time on this Honda, testing only one adjuster at a time.

**That sounds like shock damping fading as it heats up.** Oil thinning can reduce damping, but a pronounced change from controlled cold to soft and bouncy hot warrants checking the shock—not fitting a stiffer spring or winding in clickers.

Most likely is tired oil or worn internal sealing; low nitrogen charge and oil aeration are another possibility. Both can let the shock compress too easily and rebound without control once hot. Cooling back to normal supports a heat-related fault but doesn't identify which one.

**First, with the bike cool, engine off and securely supported, inspect the shock shaft, seal area and reservoir for oil or damage.** Note when it was last serviced. A dry shock can still have an internal fault, so have a suspension shop check its charge, oil and internal sealing before further hard riding. Honda specifically calls for checking nitrogen loss if rear ride height drops after riding; that drop hasn't been established here.

Don't ride it while the rear is bouncing uncontrollably. Don't open the pressurized reservoir yourself.
Soft and bouncy only after 20 minutes points to heat-related damping fade, not a spring problem. Check for leakage first; don't chase it with clickers.

Yes—the tires absorb the first part of every bump, so pressure can make the suspension feel harsh or soft without touching a clicker.

- **Higher pressure:** firmer feel, more deflection over chop, but better rim protection on rocks, square edges and hard landings.
- **Lower pressure:** more compliance and grip, but too low feels vague or squirmy and risks pinch flats and rim damage.

Honda’s baseline for your 2023 CRF450R is **100 kPa (15 psi) cold, front and rear**. Set that before judging the suspension. As general tuning practice, adjust only one tire by about **1 psi at a time**: lower for smooth slick dirt or deep sand, higher for sharp impacts. Ride the same section to compare; stop lowering at the first rim strike or squirm.

Check pressures cold at the track. Don’t bleed a hot tire back down to the cold baseline—pressure naturally rises as it heats.

**Your shock spring is likely too soft for your weight.** Getting rider sag to 105 mm has taken enough preload that the rear barely settles under the bike’s own weight.

GASGAS specifies **105 mm rider sag and 35 mm static sag**. Your 20 mm static sag is 15 mm short. Assuming the linkage moves freely and the measurements repeat, that points toward a stiffer shock spring—not a clicker change. Simply backing off preload will increase static sag but also put rider sag beyond its target.

Recheck both measurements using the same axle-to-fender points, settling the rear from both directions; noticeably different readings suggest linkage or seal friction. Once a stiffer spring is fitted, reset rider sag to 105 mm and confirm static sag comes close to 35 mm.

On your 2023 CRF450R’s **standard shock spring 56 N/mm, anything shorter than 222.9 mm (8.78 in) installed length is too much preload**. Measure the spring seat-to-seat with the rear wheel off the ground—not the exposed shock threads.

Honda’s allowed installed-length range is **222.9–233 mm**, with **232.3 mm (9.15 in)** standard. Shortening the spring adds preload and reduces sag; lengthening it does the opposite. One adjuster turn changes spring length by **1.5 mm**—that is not 1.5 mm of rider sag.

Aim for **105 mm rider sag** on the standard spring. If you still have too much sag at the shortest allowed spring length, you need a stiffer spring, not more preload. Preload changes ride height; it does not stiffen the spring rate.

Also check free sag with you off the bike: very little free sag after setting rider sag points to a spring that’s too soft. Honda publishes no free-sag target for this bike; **roughly 30–40 mm is general tuning guidance**, not Honda’s specification. These installed-length limits apply only to the standard spring.
On your 2023 CRF450R’s standard shock spring, preload is too much if installed spring length falls below 222.9 mm. Use sag—not a universal preload number—to decide whether the spring suits you.

**Most often it’s how or when you measure it.** Different gear, fuel, mud on the bike, rider position, or cold-versus-just-ridden measurements can all move the reading.

Check in this order:
1. **Repeat the measurement consistently:** same gear, fuel load, upright bike and rider position. Honda’s standard race sag is **105 mm (4.1 in)** with the standard shock spring. Measure from the center of the left rear-fender bolt to the center of the chain-adjuster locknut, first with the rear wheel off the ground, then rider aboard.
2. **Check for sticking:** take the rider-aboard reading after pushing the rear down, then again after lifting it and letting it settle. Different readings point toward friction in the linkage, swingarm or shock—not a preload adjustment.
3. **Check the preload lock rings:** mark their position and see whether they move between rides. A new spring can also settle initially; continued drift needs checking.

Honda publishes no static-sag target for this bike; recording rider-off sag alongside race sag helps separate measurement changes from mechanical changes. Don’t ride if you find loose hardware, bearing play or a shock leak.

How many millimeters does it change, measured cold under the same conditions?
Changing sag usually comes from inconsistent measuring conditions, suspension friction, or a preload collar moving—not a spring changing rate between rides.

**Bleed the forks after practice and between motos**, with the front wheel off the ground and the forks fully extended.

1. Let the forks cool, then put the bike securely on a stand so the front wheel hangs free.
2. Clean around the small air-release screw on top of each fork leg.
3. Slowly loosen each release screw to let trapped air hiss out—do not loosen the large fork cap or the damping adjuster.
4. Once the hissing stops, gently reseat each screw. Don’t overtighten them.

Your CRF450R has coil-spring forks: you’re releasing unwanted pressure, **not setting an air-spring pressure**. Built-up air can make the forks feel firmer as you ride.

For the guided job, tap **“Working on the bike?”** above the message box and choose **“Release built-up air from the fork.”**
Bleed built-up fork air after practice and between motos, with the front wheel off the ground and the forks fully extended.

**Don’t loosen the air-side cap until the main air spring has been depressurised by the correct service procedure.** The small bleeder screw only vents the outer chamber—it does not empty the pressurised air spring.

For routine care on your 2023 MC 250F:
1. With the fork cold, put the bike on a secure stand with the front wheel off the ground.
2. Loosen the small bleeder screw on each fork leg to release trapped outer-chamber pressure, then close both screws.
3. Check the main air-spring pressure with a suspension pump. GASGAS’s stock reference is **10.4 bar (151 psi)**.
4. Clean the dust boots and tubes; keep oil and cleaner off the brake disc. A leaking oil seal needs checking before riding.

**An air fork uses compressed air instead of a steel coil spring to support the bike and rider. Both still use oil to control movement.**

- **Coil-spring fork inside:** a steel coil compresses as the fork moves down. With a straight-rate spring, its force builds roughly evenly through the stroke. Trapped air above the oil adds extra resistance near bottoming.
- **Damping in both:** oil flows through pistons, valves and shim stacks to control compression and rebound. The spring supports the load; the damping stops it bouncing uncontrollably.

Air saves weight and makes support easy to adjust; coils need fewer pressure checks and are less sensitive to temperature. Neither design automatically guarantees better damping.

**A leak-down test tells you where cylinder pressure is escaping—not just whether cranking pressure is low.**

**Squish is the gap between the piston crown and the outer band of the cylinder head when the piston is at top dead center.** As the piston comes up, that band squeezes mixture toward the spark plug, creating turbulence that helps it burn faster and more evenly.

- **Too tight:** the piston can touch the head as parts heat up and stretch at high rpm. Changes that also raise compression can increase detonation risk.

3. On a closed course with clear runoff, hold the chosen opening steadily long enough for the engine to settle. Don’t force a long wide-open run if space is limited.
4. At the end, **press the kill switch and pull the clutch simultaneously**, close the throttle, and coast to a safe stop. Don’t restart or idle back.

**Go sintered for your CRF250R**—the better all-round choice for motocross, especially in mud, water and hard braking.

1. **Rear sag:** set **105 mm (4.1 in)** wearing your riding gear, with race fuel aboard. 2. **Tires:** both **100 kPa (15 psi), cold**.

**Suspension set for your weight and vet pace—not more engine power—makes the biggest difference.** On the 2023 450 SX-F, I’d spend in this order:

Testers consistently describe the 2023 chassis as stiff, particularly before it settles in.
2. **If it still beats up your hands, prioritize the fork.** A rider-specific revalve is the lower-cost route; a **WP 6500 coil-cartridge conversion** is a common comfort choice for more consistent action and better small-bump compliance. 3. **Fit the cockpit.** Set bar position and lever reach so you can stand with relaxed hands and bent elbows. Don’t automatically fit tall bars—they can make weighting the front harder.

What do you weigh in riding gear? That decides the fork-air direction and whether the shock spring needs changing before spending on valving.
